title: Corporation tax rate
description: Change the rates of corporation tax on company profits (25% main rate, 19% small profits rate), in percentage points.

baselinePolicy.text: Main rate 25% on profits over £250,000; small profits rate 19% up to £50,000 with marginal relief between.

level.label: Main rate of corporation tax
level.note: 25% since April 2023; 19% in 2022. The 19% small profits rate is unchanged by this lever.

rows.label: Increase Corporation tax by 1 percentage point

uprating.head: onshoreCorporationTax
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR March 2026 forecast for this receipts head (ADR-0004).

caveats: HMRC publishes the yield of a 1 point increase; a cut is assumed to cost the same per point, following HMRC's guidance that rate changes scale roughly linearly.

HMRC's estimates are on its Spring Statement 2025 indexed baseline for an April 2026 start. This tool shifts the profile to the chosen start year and scales it by the growth of the relevant OBR receipts head in the March 2026 forecast; the underlying level is not rebased. HMRC deferred its 2026 edition to review key assumptions.

considerations.text: HMRC's direct estimate leaves out effects on investment and the wider economy, which HMRC says are usually captured in the OBR's economy forecast.

HMRC's figure is a direct effect on this tax and closely related tax bases. It includes HMRC's standard behavioural response (for personal taxes, through taxable income elasticities and tax-motivated incorporation), but not wider effects on the economy such as inflation or investment, which HMRC says are usually captured in the OBR's economy forecast instead.

HMRC postponed the 2026 edition of these estimates (due 7 July 2026) to complete a review of the key assumptions behind some of them, after the Office for Statistics Regulation asked for more transparency about pre- and post-behavioural estimates. The figures here are HMRC's June 2025 estimates.

interactions.text: Employer costs and company profits interact: a change to one alters the base of the other.
